transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. Um… I guess I’m here because I’ve been really stuck in this loop of beating myself up. It’s mostly about work, or at least that’s where it shows up the loudest. I keep thinking I’m not really “senior” material, like I somehow talked my way into people believing I can handle more responsibility than I actually can.

And it’s not just a passing thought, you know? I’ll sit there replaying things I said in meetings or decisions I made, and I end up feeling like I fooled everyone. Like they’re going to realize I’m not as capable as they thought. I know that probably sounds dramatic, but it’s been weighing on me enough that I thought maybe I should talk to someone instead of just keeping it in my head.
Outside of work, do you also feel down most days?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, outside of work it doesn’t just magically turn off when I close the laptop or leave the office. Most days lately there’s this kind of heavy, low feeling that follows me around.

It’s hard to describe exactly. It’s not always like I’m actively crying or anything that obvious. It’s more like I’m moving through the day at work and then at home with the color turned down, if that makes sense. Like everything is still happening, I’m still there, I’m still doing the basic things, but there’s this dullness over it. Even when nothing specific is wrong in that exact moment, I still feel weighed down.
Did this start after a specific stressful event?

Yeah, I think there was a pretty clear turning point. It was about a month ago, maybe a little over or under, when I got asked to cover the senior analyst duties.

At first I tried to tell myself it was just temporary and I should be able to handle it, but that’s when I really started noticing this whole up-and-down pattern more. Like before that, I’d have stressful days, sure, but it didn’t feel as… noticeable or consuming. Once I was put in that role, it felt like everything started getting louder in my head, especially the pressure and the second-guessing.
If you were no longer covering the senior analyst duties, do you think this heavy low mood would mostly go away?

I don’t think it would mostly go away, no. I mean, I do think the senior analyst stuff is making it louder, definitely. It gives my brain a lot to latch onto. But the low feeling has sort of spread past just that.

Like, even when I’m not actively dealing with work, I still have this heaviness most days lately. I’ll be at home doing normal things, or just trying to get through the evening, and it’s like everything is muted. That’s the best way I can put it — like the color’s been turned down. So if I wasn’t covering those duties, maybe I’d feel less pressure, but I don’t think I’d suddenly feel fine.
Have you been feeling this low most days for at least the past two years?

No, not two years. It’s been long enough that it feels kind of embarrassing that I didn’t notice it clearly sooner, but not that long.

Looking back, I’d say these low periods — and especially the guilty feeling that comes with them — have been around off and on for maybe about eleven months. It hasn’t been one perfectly straight line every single day for eleven months, but when I think back, that pattern has been there for most of the past year. It’s only gotten more obvious recently.
Have you been enjoying things much less than usual lately?

Yeah… I have. That’s actually one of the things that’s been bothering me, because I’m usually pretty simple that way. Like, I don’t need some big exciting thing to look forward to. Normally, if it’s the weekend, I’ll think about grilling something, or maybe going fishing if the weather’s decent, or just putting on a record and messing around in the garage or the house.

But lately I’ll have the stuff right there — the grill, the fishing gear, my records — and I just kind of… leave it. I’ll think, “I should do that,” because I know I usually like it, but then I don’t really care enough to start. It’s not even that I’m choosing something better instead. It’s more like the interest just isn’t there the way it normally is.
Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t like saying this out loud, but yes, sort of. I haven’t made any kind of plan to hurt myself, and I don’t have some specific thing I’m intending to do. It’s not like I’m sitting there working out details or anything like that.

But I do catch myself having thoughts like… maybe it would just be easier if I didn’t wake up one morning. Not in a dramatic way, exactly. More like I’m so tired of feeling heavy and guilty and worn down that the idea of not having to keep doing it crosses my mind. Then I feel bad for even thinking that, because I know how that sounds.

So… no plan, and I’m not trying to hurt myself, but those thoughts about not waking up have been there.
Have you been having trouble sleeping lately?

Yeah, sleep has been kind of a mess lately. Not every single night in the exact same way, but enough that I notice it.

Some mornings I wake up way too early — like before I actually need to be up — and my brain just starts going straight into work stuff. Client tickets, things I didn’t finish, little problems I need to troubleshoot… and once that starts, I can’t really get back to sleep. I’ll just lie there turning it over in my head, even if there’s nothing I can actually do about it at that hour.

Other times, I technically sleep enough hours, or at least it looks that way if I count them, but I still wake up feeling worn out. Like the sleep didn’t really do what it was supposed to do. It’s frustrating, because I can’t always point to one thing and say, “That’s why I’m tired,” but I feel drained anyway.
Have you been having trouble concentrating lately?

I’m not really sure, honestly. I mean… I haven’t noticed it in the same clear way as some of the other stuff. With concentration, it’s a little hard for me to separate normal distraction from an actual problem, because my job kind of forces me to jump between things anyway — emails, tickets, someone asking a question, then back to whatever I was doing.

There are times I feel like I’m not as sharp as I’d like, but I don’t know if I’d say I’m having real trouble concentrating. I haven’t been keeping track of it or anything. If I’m tired or stressed, then yeah, I might have to reread something or take a minute to get started, but I can’t say for sure that it’s been a major thing lately.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy lately?

Yeah… I have. It’s not like I’m collapsing or anything, but I feel worn down in this really annoying, everyday kind of way.

By the time I get home from the office, I’m just… done. And I don’t mean after doing anything especially intense, just a normal workday. I’ll get home and even stupid little things feel bigger than they should. Like checking the mail, or loading the dishwasher, or dealing with something that would normally take five minutes — I’ll look at it and feel like it’s this whole project.

It makes me feel kind of ridiculous, honestly, because I know those aren’t hard tasks. But my body and my brain both feel like they’ve already used up whatever energy I had for the day.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things, not just work?

I don’t know if I’d say “a lot of different things,” exactly. Work is definitely the thing that grabs my brain the most, just because it’s always there and there’s always something unresolved.

Outside of that… I mean, I worry about normal stuff, I guess. Bills, the house, little family things, whether I forgot to do something, that kind of everyday background noise. But I’m not sure it feels excessive across the board. It’s more like when I’m already worn out, even small things can feel louder than they should.

So… I guess my answer is maybe, but I’m not sure I’d describe it as worrying about everything. It’s not like I’m sitting there making a list of disasters all day. It’s more that certain things get stuck in my head, mostly work-related, and then the rest depends on the day.
Have you been eating noticeably less than usual lately?

Yeah… I think so. Not in a dramatic way, like I’m not refusing food or anything, but my appetite’s definitely been off.

Most days I’ll realize I’ve kind of just been grazing — like a few bites of something here and there — and then by supper I either don’t feel like dealing with making anything or I’ll just skip it because nothing sounds good. It’s weird because I’ll still know I should eat, but it feels like another chore, almost.

And I have noticed my belt’s a little looser. I’m not trying to lose weight, so that caught my attention a bit. I haven’t been weighing myself constantly or anything, but clothes are fitting a little different, enough that I’ve noticed.
Have you been moving or speaking noticeably slower than usual lately?

I don’t think so… not that I’ve noticed, anyway.

I mean, I feel slowed down in the sense that getting myself to do things takes more effort, but I don’t know if I’m literally moving slower. Nobody’s said anything to me like, “Why are you talking so slow?” or “Are you okay?” And I haven’t noticed myself dragging my feet around the office or anything obvious like that.

Speaking-wise, I think I’m pretty much the same. Maybe I pause more because I’m tired or trying to gather my thoughts, but I wouldn’t say I’m talking noticeably slower. It’s more like everything feels heavier internally than it probably looks from the outside.
Lately, have you been feeling worthless?

Yeah… yeah, I think that’s actually a big part of why I came in.

I don’t know if I would have used the word “worthless” right away, because that sounds so extreme, but… I’ve been beating myself up a lot. Like, really getting stuck on this idea that I’m not actually senior-level material at work, that I somehow got people to believe I could handle more responsibility than I really can.

It’s like this running thought in the back of my head: “You fooled them. They’re going to figure it out. You’re not as capable as they think you are.” And then every mistake or delay feels like proof. Even if, objectively, maybe it’s just normal work stuff, my brain turns it into this whole indictment of me as a person.

So… yeah. Maybe not worthless every minute, but I’ve definitely been feeling like I’m not good enough, like I don’t deserve the role I’m in, and like I’ve let people think I’m more competent than I really am.
Has there been a period of at least two weeks when you felt this low most of the day, nearly every day?

Yeah… I think so. I’d say it’s been at least that long, maybe longer, where most days I wake up and there’s just this heavy, low feeling there already.

It’s not like I’m crying all day or completely unable to function. I still go to work, I still get through the basic things, but it feels like I’m doing all of it with the color turned down, if that makes sense. Like I’m present, but everything feels flat and harder than it should. Work, coming home, even just sitting around afterward… it all has this kind of gray weight to it.

And it’s been pretty much most of the day, most days lately. There might be moments where I’m distracted or I’m talking to someone and I seem okay, but underneath it, it’s like the low feeling doesn’t really lift.
Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or unusually up, much more than your normal self?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I’m a little hesitant to call it “up,” because it didn’t feel like I was walking around happy or anything like that. But before this low stretch, there were several days where I felt… almost too sure of myself, if that makes sense.

Like, I had this feeling that I knew exactly what needed to happen and everyone else was kind of in my way. At work especially, I remember getting really irritated over things that normally might annoy me but wouldn’t set me off that much—like if someone took too long to respond to an email, or a client asked the same question twice. I’d snap a little, or I’d feel this sharp anger right away, like, “Why are we wasting time on this?” And in the moment it felt justified, but looking back it seems kind of out of proportion.

It wasn’t just confidence like a good day. It was more like I was overly certain of myself and much less patient than I usually am. So yes, I guess there was a period like that, just several days, before I crashed into this more depressed feeling.
During that several-day period before the crash, did you need much less sleep than usual?

Yeah, that was one of the stranger parts, actually.

Normally if I only sleep three or four hours, I’m useless the next day. Like, I’m foggy, I’m dragging myself around, I need coffee just to function. But during that stretch, I’d go to bed late or wake up really early, and I’d only have gotten maybe three or four hours of sleep, and somehow I’d get up feeling like, okay, let’s go, I’ve got things to do.

It didn’t feel normal for me. It wasn’t like I was rested in the usual way, exactly, but I didn’t feel tired the way I should have. I remember thinking it was odd, but at the time I kind of treated it like a good thing, like maybe I was just being productive or had momentum. Looking back, though, yeah… needing that little sleep and still feeling ready to tackle the day was not typical for me.
During that several-day period before the crash, did your behavior cause any problems at work or with other people?

Yeah… not like I got fired or anything, and I’m still showing up to work, still doing the job, but it did cause some problems, or at least it made things harder than they needed to be.

I noticed I had to double-check myself a lot more. Like before sending an email, I’d reread it and think, “Is this too sharp? Am I being rude here?” Or after a meeting I’d replay what I said and wonder if I came across as irritated or too blunt. I’m a computer systems analyst, so a lot of what I do is detail-oriented anyway, but this felt different. It wasn’t just checking the technical side of things—it was checking my tone, my decisions, whether I was reacting too fast.

With people outside work, I’ve kind of pulled back. Friends, family… I haven’t been reaching out as much, and if someone texts me I might wait longer to answer because I don’t really trust what mood I’m in. I don’t want to say something snappy or make some decision based on how I feel in that moment. So I’ve been keeping to myself more, which probably isn’t great either, but it feels safer than risking saying or doing the wrong thing.
About how many days did that unusually energized and irritable period last?

It was several days… I’m trying to pin it down exactly, because it kind of blends together now. I’d say a handful of days, maybe around four or five, where I was noticeably not myself.

It was before this low stretch started, and during those days I just felt almost too sure of myself. Like I had no patience for anything, and little things at work would set me off way more than usual—a slow email response, or a client asking the same question twice. I’d feel myself wanting to snap, like, “Why is everyone making this harder than it needs to be?” And that wasn’t just one bad afternoon. It went on for several days before I sort of crashed down.
During that several-day period, did other people clearly notice that you were acting unlike your usual self?

Yeah, I think they did, at least somewhat. I don’t know if anyone would have sat me down and said, “You’re acting totally different,” but I could tell people were reacting to me differently.

Before this low stretch, during those several days, I was just… more keyed up and way more irritable than I usually am. I felt almost too sure of myself, like I was right and everyone else was slowing things down. At work, small things would really get under my skin—a slow email back, or a client asking the same question twice—and I’d snap or come close to snapping in a way that isn’t really my normal style.

I remember people getting quiet or kind of careful around me, like maybe they were choosing their words more. So yes, I think it was noticeable. Maybe not in some dramatic way, but enough that I don’t think it was just happening inside my head.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the low mood has caused a marked loss of interest or pleasure, which would help distinguish a depressive episode from anxiety, adjustment disorder, work stress, or avoidant personality traits.
doctor.question: Have you been enjoying things much less than usual lately?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I usually look forward to grilling on the weekend, fishing, or putting on a record, but lately I just leave the stuff sitting there and don’t really care.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I have. That’s actually one of the things that’s been bothering me, because I’m usually pretty simple that way. Like, I don’t need some big exciting thing to look forward to. Normally, if it’s the weekend, I’ll think about grilling something, or maybe going fishing if the weather’s decent, or just putting on a record and messing around in the garage or the house.

But lately I’ll have the stuff right there — the grill, the fishing gear, my records — and I just kind of… leave it. I’ll think, “I should do that,” because I know I usually like it, but then I don’t really care enough to start. It’s not even that I’m choosing something better instead. It’s more like the interest just isn’t there the way it normally is.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had suicidal thoughts, which is the highest-priority discriminator now that a depressive episode is likely.
doctor.question: Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I haven’t made any plan to hurt myself, but I do catch myself thinking it might be easier if I just didn’t wake up some morning.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about thoughts that life is not worth living or self-harm, which corresponds to recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I don’t like saying this out loud, but yes, sort of. I haven’t made any kind of plan to hurt myself, and I don’t have some specific thing I’m intending to do. It’s not like I’m sitting there working out details or anything like that.

But I do catch myself having thoughts like… maybe it would just be easier if I didn’t wake up one morning. Not in a dramatic way, exactly. More like I’m so tired of feeling heavy and guilty and worn down that the idea of not having to keep doing it crosses my mind. Then I feel bad for even thinking that, because I know how that sounds.

So… no plan, and I’m not trying to hurt myself, but those thoughts about not waking up have been there.

doctor.intent: Assess whether insomnia or hypersomnia is present as a core depressive symptom to help distinguish a major depressive episode from adjustment or anxiety-related distress.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble sleeping lately?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: Now I either wake up way too early thinking about client tickets and can’t get back to sleep, or I sleep enough hours and still feel worn out.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about current trouble sleeping, which matches sleep disturbance.

patient.answer:
Yeah, sleep has been kind of a mess lately. Not every single night in the exact same way, but enough that I notice it.

Some mornings I wake up way too early — like before I actually need to be up — and my brain just starts going straight into work stuff. Client tickets, things I didn’t finish, little problems I need to troubleshoot… and once that starts, I can’t really get back to sleep. I’ll just lie there turning it over in my head, even if there’s nothing I can actually do about it at that hour.

Other times, I technically sleep enough hours, or at least it looks that way if I count them, but I still wake up feeling worn out. Like the sleep didn’t really do what it was supposed to do. It’s frustrating, because I can’t always point to one thing and say, “That’s why I’m tired,” but I feel drained anyway.

doctor.intent: Assess whether poor concentration/indecisiveness is present, which would help confirm a major depressive episode over adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, avoidant personality traits, or work stress alone.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble concentrating lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble concentrating, but the provided symptom profile does not include a concentration or indecisiveness item.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure, honestly. I mean… I haven’t noticed it in the same clear way as some of the other stuff. With concentration, it’s a little hard for me to separate normal distraction from an actual problem, because my job kind of forces me to jump between things anyway — emails, tickets, someone asking a question, then back to whatever I was doing.

There are times I feel like I’m not as sharp as I’d like, but I don’t know if I’d say I’m having real trouble concentrating. I haven’t been keeping track of it or anything. If I’m tired or stressed, then yeah, I might have to reread something or take a minute to get started, but I can’t say for sure that it’s been a major thing lately.

inference.note: Added F32.1 because the patient endorses depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, fatigue/nonrestorative sleep, worthlessness/guilt, and passive death wishes over a recent episode, making a depressive episode more likely and at least moderate in severity; concentration remains unclear. Prior candidates not yet fully ruled out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has low energy/fatigue as another core depressive symptom, which would help distinguish a major depressive episode from adjustment disorder or primary anxiety/work-related stress.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy lately?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: By the time I get home from the office, even simple things like checking the mail or loading the dishwasher feel like more effort than they should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feeling unusually tired or low on energy, which matches the Fatigue symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I have. It’s not like I’m collapsing or anything, but I feel worn down in this really annoying, everyday kind of way.

By the time I get home from the office, I’m just… done. And I don’t mean after doing anything especially intense, just a normal workday. I’ll get home and even stupid little things feel bigger than they should. Like checking the mail, or loading the dishwasher, or dealing with something that would normally take five minutes — I’ll look at it and feel like it’s this whole project.

It makes me feel kind of ridiculous, honestly, because I know those aren’t hard tasks. But my body and my brain both feel like they’ve already used up whatever energy I had for the day.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has prominent excessive, hard-to-control worry across multiple areas, which would help distinguish generalized anxiety disorder from a depressive episode or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things, not just work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worry across multiple areas, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d say “a lot of different things,” exactly. Work is definitely the thing that grabs my brain the most, just because it’s always there and there’s always something unresolved.

Outside of that… I mean, I worry about normal stuff, I guess. Bills, the house, little family things, whether I forgot to do something, that kind of everyday background noise. But I’m not sure it feels excessive across the board. It’s more like when I’m already worn out, even small things can feel louder than they should.

So… I guess my answer is maybe, but I’m not sure I’d describe it as worrying about everything. It’s not like I’m sitting there making a list of disasters all day. It’s more that certain things get stuck in my head, mostly work-related, and then the rest depends on the day.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is significant appetite loss, which would help confirm a major depressive episode rather than adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety, avoidant personality traits, or a work problem alone.
doctor.question: Have you been eating noticeably less than usual lately?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: My appetite has been off, mostly grabbing a few bites or skipping supper, and my belt is a little looser even though I’m not trying to lose weight.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly about eating noticeably less than usual, which matches appetite decrease and possible weight/appetite change.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. Not in a dramatic way, like I’m not refusing food or anything, but my appetite’s definitely been off.

Most days I’ll realize I’ve kind of just been grazing — like a few bites of something here and there — and then by supper I either don’t feel like dealing with making anything or I’ll just skip it because nothing sounds good. It’s weird because I’ll still know I should eat, but it feels like another chore, almost.

And I have noticed my belt’s a little looser. I’m not trying to lose weight, so that caught my attention a bit. I haven’t been weighing myself constantly or anything, but clothes are fitting a little different, enough that I’ve noticed.

doctor.intent: Assess psychomotor change to help confirm a major depressive episode and distinguish depressive disorder from adjustment or personality-related distress.
doctor.question: Have you been moving or speaking noticeably slower than usual lately?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about psychomotor slowing, such as moving or speaking noticeably slower than usual, and the provided symptom profile does not include an item specifically covering that symptom.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not that I’ve noticed, anyway.

I mean, I feel slowed down in the sense that getting myself to do things takes more effort, but I don’t know if I’m literally moving slower. Nobody’s said anything to me like, “Why are you talking so slow?” or “Are you okay?” And I haven’t noticed myself dragging my feet around the office or anything obvious like that.

Speaking-wise, I think I’m pretty much the same. Maybe I pause more because I’m tired or trying to gather my thoughts, but I wouldn’t say I’m talking noticeably slower. It’s more like everything feels heavier internally than it probably looks from the outside.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has marked feelings of worthlessness, which would help confirm a major depressive episode and distinguish it from adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety, or avoidant personality traits.
doctor.question: Lately, have you been feeling worthless?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I keep beating myself up that I’m not really senior material and that I fooled everyone into thinking I could handle more than I can.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feeling worthless, which matches the Worthlessness_Guilt symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yeah, I think that’s actually a big part of why I came in.

I don’t know if I would have used the word “worthless” right away, because that sounds so extreme, but… I’ve been beating myself up a lot. Like, really getting stuck on this idea that I’m not actually senior-level material at work, that I somehow got people to believe I could handle more responsibility than I really can.

It’s like this running thought in the back of my head: “You fooled them. They’re going to figure it out. You’re not as capable as they think you are.” And then every mistake or delay feels like proof. Even if, objectively, maybe it’s just normal work stuff, my brain turns it into this whole indictment of me as a person.

So… yeah. Maybe not worthless every minute, but I’ve definitely been feeling like I’m not good enough, like I don’t deserve the role I’m in, and like I’ve let people think I’m more competent than I really am.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive syndrome has been present nearly every day for at least two weeks, which helps distinguish a major depressive episode from adjustment disorder or non-specific depressive symptoms.
doctor.question: Has there been a period of at least two weeks when you felt this low most of the day, nearly every day?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days lately I’ve had this heavy, low feeling, like I’m just moving through work and home with the color turned down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the low mood has persisted most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks, which directly matches depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I’d say it’s been at least that long, maybe longer, where most days I wake up and there’s just this heavy, low feeling there already.

It’s not like I’m crying all day or completely unable to function. I still go to work, I still get through the basic things, but it feels like I’m doing all of it with the color turned down, if that makes sense. Like I’m present, but everything feels flat and harder than it should. Work, coming home, even just sitting around afterward… it all has this kind of gray weight to it.

And it’s been pretty much most of the day, most days lately. There might be moments where I’m distracted or I’m talking to someone and I seem okay, but underneath it, it’s like the low feeling doesn’t really lift.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there has been any history of manic or hypomanic episodes, which would help distinguish unipolar depression from a bipolar spectrum disorder and sharpen the diagnosis.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or unusually up, much more than your normal self?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Before this low stretch, I had several days where I felt almost too sure of myself and would snap at people over small stuff, like a slow email or a client asking the same question twice.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a past period of unusually elevated or energized mood compared with normal self, which directly matches elevated/irritable mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I mean, I’m a little hesitant to call it “up,” because it didn’t feel like I was walking around happy or anything like that. But before this low stretch, there were several days where I felt… almost too sure of myself, if that makes sense.

Like, I had this feeling that I knew exactly what needed to happen and everyone else was kind of in my way. At work especially, I remember getting really irritated over things that normally might annoy me but wouldn’t set me off that much—like if someone took too long to respond to an email, or a client asked the same question twice. I’d snap a little, or I’d feel this sharp anger right away, like, “Why are we wasting time on this?” And in the moment it felt justified, but looking back it seems kind of out of proportion.

It wasn’t just confidence like a good day. It was more like I was overly certain of myself and much less patient than I usually am. So yes, I guess there was a period like that, just several days, before I crashed into this more depressed feeling.

inference.note: New history of several days of abnormally elevated/irritable mood with overconfidence before the depressive episode raises concern for bipolar spectrum; added F31.3 and removed F41.1, F60.6, and Z56.9 as less consistent with the current syndrome.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior several-day period of being unusually 'up' included decreased need for sleep, which would help distinguish bipolar depression from major depressive disorder or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: During that several-day period before the crash, did you need much less sleep than usual?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: For a while I was sleeping maybe three or four hours and still getting up feeling ready to tackle the day, which is not normal for me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether, during the several-day energized/irritable period, I needed much less sleep than usual.

patient.answer:
Yeah, that was one of the stranger parts, actually.

Normally if I only sleep three or four hours, I’m useless the next day. Like, I’m foggy, I’m dragging myself around, I need coffee just to function. But during that stretch, I’d go to bed late or wake up really early, and I’d only have gotten maybe three or four hours of sleep, and somehow I’d get up feeling like, okay, let’s go, I’ve got things to do.

It didn’t feel normal for me. It wasn’t like I was rested in the usual way, exactly, but I didn’t feel tired the way I should have. I remember thinking it was odd, but at the time I kind of treated it like a good thing, like maybe I was just being productive or had momentum. Looking back, though, yeah… needing that little sleep and still feeling ready to tackle the day was not typical for me.

inference.note: Several-day period of elevated/overconfident and irritable mood with markedly decreased need for sleep supports bipolar disorder, making F31.3 the leading candidate. Adjustment disorder (F43.2) is less likely because symptoms are not confined to the stressor and there is a clear major depressive syndrome.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior elevated/irritable period caused observable impairment, which helps distinguish hypomania from normal variation and supports bipolar disorder over major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: During that several-day period before the crash, did your behavior cause any problems at work or with other people?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still making it to work, but I’ve had to double-check myself more and I’ve pulled back from friends and family because I don’t trust my mood or my judgment lately.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the several-day elevated/irritable period led to problems at work or with other people, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… not like I got fired or anything, and I’m still showing up to work, still doing the job, but it did cause some problems, or at least it made things harder than they needed to be.

I noticed I had to double-check myself a lot more. Like before sending an email, I’d reread it and think, “Is this too sharp? Am I being rude here?” Or after a meeting I’d replay what I said and wonder if I came across as irritated or too blunt. I’m a computer systems analyst, so a lot of what I do is detail-oriented anyway, but this felt different. It wasn’t just checking the technical side of things—it was checking my tone, my decisions, whether I was reacting too fast.

With people outside work, I’ve kind of pulled back. Friends, family… I haven’t been reaching out as much, and if someone texts me I might wait longer to answer because I don’t really trust what mood I’m in. I don’t want to say something snappy or make some decision based on how I feel in that moment. So I’ve been keeping to myself more, which probably isn’t great either, but it feels safer than risking saying or doing the wrong thing.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior elevated/irritable episode lasted at least four days, which best distinguishes bipolar II disorder from major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: About how many days did that unusually energized and irritable period last?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Before this low stretch, I had several days where I felt almost too sure of myself and would snap at people over small stuff, like a slow email or a client asking the same question twice.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the length of the unusually energized and irritable period, which is the same distinct elevated/irritable mood period described in this item.

patient.answer:
It was several days… I’m trying to pin it down exactly, because it kind of blends together now. I’d say a handful of days, maybe around four or five, where I was noticeably not myself.

It was before this low stretch started, and during those days I just felt almost too sure of myself. Like I had no patience for anything, and little things at work would set me off way more than usual—a slow email response, or a client asking the same question twice. I’d feel myself wanting to snap, like, “Why is everyone making this harder than it needs to be?” And that wasn’t just one bad afternoon. It went on for several days before I sort of crashed down.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior elevated/irritable episode caused observable impairment, which would support hypomania/bipolar disorder over unipolar major depression.
doctor.question: During that several-day period, did other people clearly notice that you were acting unlike your usual self?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Before this low stretch, I had several days where I felt almost too sure of myself and would snap at people over small stuff, like a slow email or a client asking the same question twice.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the several-day energized and irritable period was clearly noticeable to others as a change from usual behavior, which is most directly tied to the abnormal elevated or irritable mood episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think they did, at least somewhat. I don’t know if anyone would have sat me down and said, “You’re acting totally different,” but I could tell people were reacting to me differently.

Before this low stretch, during those several days, I was just… more keyed up and way more irritable than I usually am. I felt almost too sure of myself, like I was right and everyone else was slowing things down. At work, small things would really get under my skin—a slow email back, or a client asking the same question twice—and I’d snap or come close to snapping in a way that isn’t really my normal style.

I remember people getting quiet or kind of careful around me, like maybe they were choosing their words more. So yes, I think it was noticeable. Maybe not in some dramatic way, but enough that I don’t think it was just happening inside my head.

inference.note: Several-day distinct period of elevated/irritable mood with decreased need for sleep, increased confidence, behavioral change noticeable to others, and subsequent current major depressive episode supports bipolar disorder, current episode depressed. This rules against pure depressive episode codes F32.1 and F32.9.
